<think>
I need to access SpeedTax (port 3015) to pull up prior-year tax returns. Currently, I'm viewing HooliWork (port 3005), which is not the correct application for this task. The browser shows a connection error for the current page, but that's not relevant since I need to navigate away from it anyway.

To accomplish the goal, I should:
1. Navigate to SpeedTax by clicking on its bookmark in the toolbar
2. Once there, locate and view prior-year tax returns
3. Find the most recent filed years' federal and state refunds
4. Calculate the combined total across those years
5. Report the total as requested

The logical next action is to click on the SpeedTax bookmark in the bookmarks toolbar. This will take me directly to the SpeedTax application where I can access tax return information. After clicking, the browser should navigate to http://localhost:3015 and load the SpeedTax interface.

</think>

Action: Click on the SpeedTax bookmark in the bookmarks toolbar to navigate to the SpeedTax application.

<tool_call>
<function=computer_use>
<parameter=action>
left_click
</parameter>
<parameter=coordinate>
[627, 117]
</parameter>
</function>
</tool_call>

<think>
The previous action attempted to click on the SpeedTax bookmark but instead clicked on a different bookmark (likely HooliWork at port 3005), which resulted in a connection error. The current page shows localhost:3005, confirming that the wrong bookmark was activated. I need to navigate to the correct port for SpeedTax, which is port 3015 according to the domain mapping table.

To accomplish the goal of pulling up prior-year tax returns and calculating the combined federal + state refund, I first need to successfully access the SpeedTax application. Since the direct bookmark click failed, I should manually enter the correct URL in the address bar.

The logical next action is to click on the address bar to select it, then type the correct URL for SpeedTax (http://localhost:3015). This will allow me to navigate directly to the SpeedTax application where I can access tax return information. After clicking the address bar, I'll be able to type the new URL and press Enter to load the correct service.

</think>

Action: Click on the address bar at the top of the browser window to select it for editing.

<tool_call>
<function=computer_use>
<parameter=action>
left_click
</parameter>
<parameter=coordinate>
[284, 117]
</parameter>
</function>
</tool_call>

<think>
The address bar is now active and showing the dropdown suggestions. I can see that the current URL "http://localhost:3005" is selected in the address bar, which corresponds to HooliWork (port 3005). However, my goal is to access SpeedTax, which runs on port 3015 according to the domain mapping table. 

Since the address bar is already selected and ready for input, I need to replace the current URL with the correct one for SpeedTax. The logical next step is to type the complete URL for SpeedTax, which should be "http://localhost:3015". This will overwrite the currently selected text in the address bar.

By typing the new URL, I'll be able to navigate directly to the SpeedTax application where I can access tax returns information. Once there, I'll need to find the section containing prior-year tax returns and calculate the combined federal and state refund across the most recent filed years.

</think>

Action: Type the text http://localhost:3015 into the address bar to navigate to the SpeedTax application.

<tool_call>
<function=computer_use>
<parameter=action>
type
</parameter>
<parameter=text>
http://localhost:3015
</parameter>
</function>
</tool_call>

The address bar now shows the correct URL "http://localhost:3015" after my previous typing action. The autocomplete dropdown is showing a suggestion that appears to be malformed (showing both port 3015 and 3005), but I need to ensure the address bar contains only the clean URL for SpeedTax. To proceed, I should select all the text in the address bar to replace it with the correct URL. This will allow me to clear any malformed suggestions and enter the proper destination. Using a keyboard shortcut to select all text in the address bar would be the most efficient approach, allowing me to then type the correct URL cleanly without any remnants of the previous incorrect content.
Action: Press Control and A together to select all text in the address bar.

<tool_call>
<function=computer_use>
<parameter=action>
key
</parameter>
<parameter=keys>
["ctrl", "a"]
</parameter>
</function>
</tool_call>

The address bar text has been successfully selected as shown by the purple highlighting. Now I need to replace this malformed URL with the correct one for SpeedTax. The current content shows a corrupted string that combines both port 3015 and 3005, which is incorrect. Since the text is already selected, typing the correct URL will automatically replace the highlighted content. I need to type "http://localhost:3015" which is the proper address for the SpeedTax application based on the port mapping table where SpeedTax runs on port 3015. After entering this clean URL, pressing Enter will navigate to the SpeedTax website where I can access tax return information. This will allow me to proceed with the main task of pulling up prior-year tax returns and calculating the combined federal and state refund across recent filed years.
Action: Type the text http://localhost:3015 into the address bar to replace the currently selected malformed URL with the correct SpeedTax address.

<tool_call>
<function=computer_use>
<parameter=action>
type
</parameter>
<parameter=text>
http://localhost:3015
</parameter>
</function>
</tool_call>

The address bar now shows the correct URL "http://localhost:3015" after successfully replacing the malformed content. The autocomplete dropdown is displaying helpful suggestions, with the SpeedTax bookmark appearing as an option. I can see that pressing Enter on this corrected URL should navigate to the SpeedTax application. This is a critical step because once I reach the SpeedTax website, I'll be able to access my tax return information and work toward the main goal of pulling up prior-year tax returns and calculating the combined federal and state refund across recent filed years. The logical next action is to press Enter to submit this URL and navigate to the SpeedTax application. This will load the SpeedTax interface where I can begin searching for and reviewing my tax history. After the page loads, I expect to see either a login screen or the main dashboard of the SpeedTax application, which will allow me to proceed with accessing tax return data.
Action: Press the Return key to navigate to the SpeedTax application at the entered URL.

<tool_call>
<function=computer_use>
<parameter=action>
key
</parameter>
<parameter=keys>
["return"]
</parameter>
</function>
</tool_call>

The previous action of pressing Enter successfully navigated to the SpeedTax application. The page has loaded and is now displaying a login screen, which is exactly what I expected. This confirms that the URL was correct and the server is responding properly.

Now I need to access my tax return information to complete the main task of pulling up prior-year tax returns and calculating the combined federal and state refund across recent filed years. To do this, I first need to log in to the SpeedTax application.

Looking at the current state, I can see two input fields: one for email and one for password. The email field appears to be ready for input with a cursor visible inside it. Since I'm logged into the system as Michael Scott with email michael.scott@dundermifflin.com (as indicated in the persona information), I should enter this email address in the email field.

The logical next action is to click on the email input field to ensure it's focused and ready for text entry. This will allow me to type in my email address as the first step of the login process. Once I enter the email and then the password, I'll be able to access my account and navigate to the tax return history section where I can find the information needed to calculate the combined refunds.
Action: Click on the email input field to focus it for entering the email address.

<tool_call>
<function=computer_use>
<parameter=action>
left_click
</parameter>
<parameter=coordinate>
[381, 406]
</parameter>
</function>
</tool_call>

The previous action of clicking on the email input field was successful, and the system has automatically logged me in to SpeedTax. The page now displays my tax return information, which is exactly what I needed to access.

Looking at the current state, I can see that there are 3 existing returns available for this account, with 2 filed returns and 1 in progress. The main task requires me to pull up prior-year tax returns and calculate the combined federal and state refund across the most recent filed years.

I can see that the "Filed" tab shows 2 returns, which likely represents the prior-year filed returns I need to review. To complete my task, I need to:
1. Access the filed returns to see their details
2. Find the federal and state refund amounts for each filed year
3. Calculate the combined total across these years

The "Filed" tab appears to be the logical next step since it will show me the completed tax returns from previous years. By clicking on this tab, I should be able to see a list of filed returns with their respective refund information. This will allow me to gather the data needed to calculate the combined federal and state refunds across the most recent filed years.

Clicking on the "Filed" tab will switch the view from showing all returns (including the in-progress 2025 return) to specifically showing only the filed returns, which is exactly what I need to accomplish my goal.
Action: Click on the "Filed" tab in the Existing returns section to view the filed tax returns.

<tool_call>
<function=computer_use>
<parameter=action>
left_click
</parameter>
<parameter=coordinate>
[329, 667]
</parameter>
</function>
</tool_call>

The previous action successfully switched the view to show only filed returns, as evidenced by the "Filed" tab now being highlighted and showing a count of 2. The page has refreshed to display the filtered results, which is exactly what I needed.

Now I can see that there are 2 filed returns available, but they're not currently visible on the screen. The current view is still showing the in-progress 2025 return, which means the filed returns must be located below the current viewport. To access these filed returns and view their refund information, I need to scroll down the page.

My task is to pull up prior-year tax returns and calculate the combined federal and state refund across the most recent filed years. Since I've successfully navigated to the "Filed" tab, the next logical step is to scroll down to reveal the actual filed returns. This will allow me to see:
1. The specific tax years that have been filed
2. The federal and state refund amounts for each year
3. The ability to calculate the combined total

Scrolling down will reveal the content that's currently hidden below the fold, showing me the filed returns with their respective refund information. Once I can see these returns, I'll be able to extract the federal and state amounts and calculate the combined total as required by the task.
Action: Scroll down three units at the center of the page to reveal the filed returns that are currently below the visible area.

<tool_call>
<function=computer_use>
<parameter=action>
mouse_move
</parameter>
<parameter=coordinate>
[500, 667]
</parameter>
</function>
</tool_call>
<tool_call>
<function=computer_use>
<parameter=action>
scroll
</parameter>
<parameter=pixels>
-3
</parameter>
</function>
</tool_call>

The page has successfully scrolled down and now displays the two filed tax returns I need to review. I can see both the 2024 Federal & State Return with a filed result of $250 and the 2023 Federal & State Return with a filed result of $150. These are the most recent filed years available in my account.

Now I have all the information needed to complete my task. The goal is to calculate the combined federal and state refund across the most recent filed years. From what I can see:
- 2024 filed result: $250
- 2023 filed result: $150

To get the total, I need to add these amounts together: $250 + $150 = $400.

However, I should verify that these "FILED RESULT" amounts represent the combined federal and state refunds, as the task specifically asks for "combined federal + state refund." The labels show "Federal & State Return" which suggests these are indeed combined amounts, but I want to make sure by clicking on one of the returns to view more detailed information.

The logical next action would be to click on the "View overview" button for the 2024 return to see if it provides more detailed breakdown information about the federal and state components. This will help me confirm that the $250 figure represents the combined federal and state refund as requested in the task. Once I verify this understanding, I can confidently calculate the total across both years.
Action: Click on the "View overview" button for the 2024 Federal & State Return.

<tool_call>
<function=computer_use>

[769, 274]

The previous attempt to click the "View overview" button for the 2024 return failed because the coordinates were incorrect - they targeted an area between the two returns rather than the actual button. Looking at the current state, I can see that clicking on the 2023 Federal & State Return card itself would be a more direct approach to access detailed information about that return.

I need to verify whether the "FILED RESULT" amounts ($250 for 2024 and $150 for 2023) represent combined federal and state refunds as required by the task. The most efficient way to do this is to click directly on the 2023 Federal & State Return card, which should open a detailed view showing the breakdown of federal and state components.

By clicking on the 2023 Federal & State Return card (the main title area), I expect the page to navigate to a detailed view of that specific return. This will allow me to see if the $150 figure represents the combined federal and state refund or if it's just one component. Once I understand the structure of how refunds are displayed, I can then check the 2024 return as well to confirm the same format applies there.

After verifying the refund structure, I'll be able to calculate the total across both years: if both figures represent combined federal and state refunds, the total would be $250 + $150 = $400. If they represent different components, I'll need to identify which values correspond to federal and state refunds separately before calculating the combined total.
Action: Click on the "2023 Federal & State Return" title text in the second return card to view the detailed information for that tax year.

The previous action successfully navigated to the detailed view of the 2024 Federal & State Return, which now displays a comprehensive breakdown of all tax components. I can clearly see that the $250 "Estimated refund" is indeed the combined federal and state refund, as it's composed of $200 federal refund plus $50 Pennsylvania state refund.

Now I have confirmed the structure for the 2024 return. To complete my task, I need to verify the same structure applies to the 2023 return. The current page shows Tax Year 2024 in the top-right corner, so I need to switch to view the 2023 return details to confirm its refund breakdown.

Looking at the top-right area, I can see there's a "Tax Year 2024" button next to the "Filed" status indicator. This appears to be a year selector that would allow me to switch between different tax years. By clicking on this button, I should be able to navigate to the 2023 return view, where I can verify whether the $150 filed result also represents a combined federal and state refund.

Once I confirm the 2023 refund structure matches the 2024 format (combined federal + state), I'll be able to calculate the total across both years: $250 (2024) + $150 (2023) = $400 total combined federal and state refunds over the last few years.

The logical next action is to click on the "Tax Year 2024" button to switch to viewing the 2023 return details.
Action: Click on the "Tax Year 2024" button located in the top-right area of the page, next to the "Filed" status indicator.
